laws.penalty: Discrimination on basis of sexual orientation or gender identity: complaints to AHRC or state tribunal.
exceptions: Conversion practices banned in NSW, Victoria, Queensland, ACT, SA, and WA
Religious exemptions in employment by religious bodies remain contested
Trans people can change legal gender on documents (federal and state reforms)

quiz.q: When did same-sex marriage become legal across Australia?
quiz.explanation: Same-sex marriage became legal in Australia on 9 December 2017, following the voluntary postal survey in which 61.6% voted 'yes', and the subsequent Marriage Amendment Act 2017.

laws.title: Driver's Licence — Visitors & New Residents
laws.subtitle: Foreign licences valid for 3 months; convert after taking up residency
laws.fullDescription: Overseas visitors may drive in Victoria on their foreign licence for up to 3 months from date of arrival if the licence is in English or accompanied by an accredited English translation or IDP. After 3 months, new Victorian residents must convert their licence at a VicRoads office. Licences from certain countries qualify for direct conversion; others require a knowledge and skills test.
laws.penalty: Driving without a valid licence: fine up to $2,200; vehicle may be impounded
exceptions: Diplomatic personnel with valid diplomatic IDs
Members of visiting armed forces under bilateral agreements
Short-term tourists within the 3-month window with valid foreign licence

quiz.q: How long may an overseas visitor drive in Victoria on their foreign driver's licence?
quiz.explanation: Overseas visitors may drive in Victoria on a valid foreign licence for up to 3 months from arrival. After that, new residents must convert to a VIC licence.

laws.title: Hunting & Fishing — Interstate & Overseas Visitors
laws.subtitle: Same licences apply to all — no 'non-resident' surcharge in VIC
laws.fullDescription: Victorian fishing licences: interstate visitors pay the same fees as residents. Annual: ~$35; 3-day: ~$13. VIC fishing licence does not cover NSW, QLD, or other state waters. Recreational game licence needed for deer (Open Season or Restricted Season depending on species) — same for interstate visitors. Australian states generally do not apply higher fees for interstate visitors, unlike some US states. Always check species-specific rules, bag limits, and seasonal restrictions before fishing or hunting.
laws.penalty: Fishing without a licence: fine up to $2,200; hunting without a Game Hunting Licence: fine up to $22,000
exceptions: Indigenous Australians exercising native title or traditional rights
Children under minimum age thresholds
Activities on private land with landowner permission (for some species)

quiz.q: Do interstate visitors pay higher hunting or fishing licence fees in Victoria compared to residents?
options: No — same fees apply to all
Only overseas visitors pay a higher fee
quiz.explanation: Unlike some US states, Australian states do not generally impose higher 'non-resident' licence fees. Interstate visitors pay the same as Victoria residents.

laws.title: Drink Driving Enforcement — Mid-Range & High-Range BAC
laws.subtitle: 0.05% general limit; heavier penalties above 0.08% and 0.15%
laws.fullDescription: All Australian states share the 0.05% BAC limit for fully licensed drivers. Victoria uses tiered penalties: low-range (0.05–0.079%), mid-range (0.08–0.149%), and high-range (≥0.15%). NSW conducts more than 5 million random breath tests per year — among the highest rates in Australia. Mobile RBT units operate 24/7. Mid-range (0.08–0.15) and high-range (≥0.15) BAC attract heavier penalties including mandatory interlock. Random Breath Testing (RBT) is conducted without suspicion of impairment — any driver can be stopped.
laws.penalty: Low-range: $561 fine + 3 demerit points; Mid-range: $818 fine, 6-month disqualification (first offence at 0.07–0.15 BAC); mandatory behaviour change program; High-range: $3,300 fine, 3-year disqualification (first offence); mandatory interlock
exceptions: Medical conditions causing false positives are subject to challenge
Mouth alcohol (mouthwash) dissipates — 15-minute observation period before test

quiz.q: In Australia, which blood alcohol level is generally classed as 'high-range' drink driving?
quiz.explanation: Australia's high-range drink driving threshold is ≥0.15% BAC. This attracts the severest automatic penalties including long disqualifications and mandatory alcohol interlocks.

laws.title: Mandatory Seat Belts — All Occupants
laws.subtitle: Every person in a moving vehicle must be correctly restrained
laws.fullDescription: All occupants must wear an approved seatbelt at all times. Children must be restrained in an approved child seat appropriate for their age/size. The driver is responsible for ensuring passengers under 16 are correctly restrained. Seat belts have been compulsory in Australia since 1971 (VIC was the first jurisdiction in the world to make them mandatory, in 1970). Child restraint rules: rear-facing for infants, forward-facing with harness for toddlers, booster seats for children up to approximately 145cm.
laws.penalty: $387 fine + 3 demerit points per unbelted occupant (driver responsible for passengers under 16)
exceptions: Reversing a vehicle at low speed on private property
Medical exemption certificate holders
Emergency services personnel performing specific operational duties

quiz.q: Who was the first jurisdiction in the world to make seat belts compulsory?
quiz.explanation: Victoria, Australia introduced mandatory seat belt laws in 1970 — the first jurisdiction in the world to do so. All Australian states now require all occupants to be belted.

laws.title: School Zone Speed Limit — 40 km/h
laws.subtitle: Reduced speed applies during school drop-off and pick-up times
laws.fullDescription: School zones in Victoria require drivers to slow to 40 km/h during active school hours. School zones operate at 40 km/h on school days 8:00–9:30 am and 2:30–4:00 pm. Victoria also has "High Pedestrian Activity Areas" at 40 km/h in some CBD areas. School zones are typically marked with fluorescent yellow/green signs and, in many locations, flashing amber lights to indicate when the limit is active. Increased demerit points often apply during double-demerit periods.
laws.penalty: $409 fine + 3 demerit points
exceptions: Vehicles responding to emergency calls (sirens/lights active)
School buses loading/unloading at designated stops (separate rules apply)

quiz.q: What is the school zone speed limit in Victoria?
quiz.explanation: In Victoria, the school zone speed limit is 40 km/h. Most Australian states use 40 km/h in school zones.

laws.title: Move Over / Slow Down — Emergency & Breakdown Vehicles
laws.subtitle: Slow to 40 km/h when passing stationary emergency vehicles
laws.fullDescription: Under Victoria's road rules, drivers must slow to 40 km/h (or less if safe) when passing stationary or slow-moving emergency vehicles (police, ambulance, fire), tow trucks, and road maintenance vehicles displaying flashing lights. Where a dividing median exists, this obligation does not apply (opposite-lane vehicles not affected). Drivers must slow to 40 km/h when passing stationary or slow-moving emergency vehicles, tow trucks, or road maintenance vehicles displaying blue, red, or amber flashing lights. This applies on roads without a dividing barrier.
laws.penalty: $409 fine + 3 demerit points
exceptions: Vehicles in the opposite lane separated by a physical median barrier
Emergency vehicles in the same direction travelling at normal speed

quiz.q: What must drivers do when passing a stationary police car with lights flashing on a road without a dividing median in Victoria?
options: Slow to 40 km/h and pass carefully
Move to the opposite lane at any speed
quiz.explanation: In Victoria, drivers must slow to 40 km/h when passing stationary emergency or breakdown vehicles with lights flashing, where there is no dividing barrier. Failure to do so attracts a significant fine and demerit points.

laws.title: Rental Car Insurance — Damage Liability & Coverage
laws.subtitle: No mandatory rental insurance law; renters liable for vehicle damage by default
laws.fullDescription: Australian law does not require renters to purchase the rental company's Collision Damage Waiver (CDW) or Loss Damage Waiver (LDW). Australian law does not mandate that renters purchase rental company insurance (CDW/LDW). All rental vehicles include compulsory third-party (CTP) insurance for personal injury. Renters are personally liable for damage to the vehicle unless they purchase the hire company's damage cover or hold a credit card/travel policy that covers rental car excess. Renters should check whether their credit card (gold/platinum cards often include rental cover) or travel insurance policy covers vehicle damage and excess before declining the hire company's optional cover. Third-party injury is covered by the vehicle's compulsory third-party (CTP) policy.
laws.penalty: Unreduced excess liability: Standard excess: $2,000–$5,000 (reducible to $0 with purchased waiver); Damage to third-party vehicles: covered by CTP (personal injury) but own vehicle damage is renter's liability without CDW
exceptions: CTP/green slip covers third-party personal injury regardless of whether CDW is purchased
Credit card or travel insurance may cover rental excess — check policy before travel
laws.sourceLabel: ACCC Car Hire Guide / State Fair Trading

quiz.q: What does a standard Australian rental vehicle's compulsory third-party (CTP) insurance cover?
options: Personal injury to other people involved in a crash
quiz.explanation: CTP (compulsory third-party) insurance covers personal injury to other parties in a crash — not damage to the rental vehicle itself. Renters are personally liable for vehicle damage unless they purchase additional cover.

laws.title: Toll Roads & Electronic Payment — e-TAG Required
laws.subtitle: Cashless tolling via Linkt / CityLink / EastLink — no cash booths on Australian toll roads
laws.fullDescription: All tolled roads in Australia are cashless. Victoria has major tolled motorways including CityLink and EastLink in Melbourne. All are cashless — e-TAG (Linkt) or online payment registration within 3 days required. Pass products available for occasional users. Linkt accounts work nationally and can be opened online or at service stations. Visitors can purchase short-term passes. Hiring a car that includes a toll pass is recommended for city driving in Sydney or Melbourne.
laws.penalty: Unpaid tolls: original toll + $10–$15 administrative fee; escalating penalties for repeat non-payment including referral to debt collectors; possible licence suspension
exceptions: Motorcycles are exempt from tolls in NSW and VIC
Some toll roads have discounts for e-TAG users vs. video tolling
Emergency vehicles on duty are exempt

quiz.q: How are tolls paid on Australian toll roads?
options: E-TAG or online registration of number plate
quiz.explanation: All Australian toll roads are fully cashless. Payment is via e-TAG (Linkt) or by registering your number plate online within 3 days of travel. There are no cash booths on any Australian toll road.

laws.title: Left Turn on Red — Generally Prohibited in Australia
laws.subtitle: Unlike North America, Australia does NOT permit left turn on red at most intersections
laws.fullDescription: In Australia (where traffic drives on the left), the equivalent of a 'right turn on red' in North America is a 'left turn on red'. This is NOT permitted as a general rule anywhere in Australia. Unlike some US states, Australia does NOT permit a free left turn on red as a general rule. Drivers must stop and wait for a green signal. Some intersections display a "Left Turn on Red Permitted When Safe" sign — only at those specific locations may drivers turn left on red after giving way. Visitors from North America or other left-turn-on-red jurisdictions should note this critical difference to avoid fines.
laws.penalty: Disobeying a red light: $464 fine + 3 demerit points (6 during double-demerit periods)
exceptions: Intersections with a specific 'Left Turn on Red Permitted When Safe' sign
Emergency vehicles responding to emergencies

quiz.q: Can you turn left at a red light in Australia (as you can turn right on red in the US)?
options: Yes — only if a sign says so
quiz.explanation: In Australia, left turns on red are NOT permitted as a general rule (unlike right-on-red in the US). Only specific intersections with a 'Left Turn on Red Permitted When Safe' sign allow this manoeuvre.

laws.title: Transit Lanes (Transit lanes (T2/T3)) — Minimum Occupancy Required
laws.subtitle: T2 = 2+ occupants; T3 = 3+ occupants; also open to buses, taxis, motorcycles
laws.fullDescription: Victoria uses transit lanes (T2 and T3) to encourage carpooling and reduce peak-hour congestion. VIC transit lanes (T2/T3) require minimum 2 or 3 occupants. Also usable by taxis, buses, motorcycles. CityLink has no HOV provisions. Hours and location signposted. Motorcycles, buses, and taxis can typically use any transit lane regardless of occupancy. Bicycles may use transit lanes in some jurisdictions. Signage indicates hours of operation — some lanes operate all day, others only during peak hours.
laws.penalty: $349 fine + 2 demerit points for unauthorised use of a transit lane
exceptions: Buses (regardless of occupancy)
Taxis and rideshare vehicles (with passengers)
Motorcycles
Bicycles (where signed)

quiz.q: What does 'T3 transit lane' mean in Australia?
options: A lane requiring at least 3 vehicle occupants
A lane open 24/7 to all vehicles
A third lane on a motorway
quiz.explanation: T3 transit lanes require at least 3 occupants (including the driver). T2 lanes require at least 2. Motorcycles, buses, and taxis can use any transit lane. Unauthorised use attracts a fine and demerit points.

laws.title: Hunting Licence — Game Animals & Interstate Visitors
laws.subtitle: Game Hunting Licence required; same rules for residents and interstate visitors
laws.fullDescription: NSW requires a Game Hunting Licence (GHL) to hunt deer, wild boar, rabbits, hares, and other declared game animals on private land and some public land. Interstate visitors are subject to the same GHL requirements and fees as NSW residents. Hunting on public land (State Forests) requires a Restricted Game Hunting Licence. Hunting of native Australian animals (kangaroos, wallabies, wombats, echidnas, koalas, etc.) is strictly prohibited without a specific wildlife authority permit — these are not game animals. Feral animals (rabbits, foxes, pigs, deer where declared feral) may be hunted subject to licence and landowner permission.
laws.penalty: Hunting without a valid GHL: fine up to $22,000
exceptions: Farmers/landowners controlling feral animals on their own property (within limits)
Indigenous Australians with native title rights
Licensed professional hunters engaged for pest control

quiz.q: Can interstate visitors hunt game animals (such as deer or wild pigs) in Victoria?
options: No — non-residents are prohibited from hunting
Yes — with the same licence required of residents
Yes — no licence needed for feral animals
Yes — with a special non-resident permit costing more
quiz.explanation: Interstate visitors may hunt game animals in Victoria but must hold the same licence required of residents. Australia does not apply 'non-resident' premium fees like some US states. Hunting native wildlife without a permit is a serious offence.

laws.title: Recreational Fishing Licence — Fees & Requirements
laws.subtitle: Resident fee: $35/year or $7/day (NSW recreational fishing fee); Interstate visitor: Same as residents — no separate interstate/overseas licence
laws.fullDescription: A NSW Recreational Fishing Fee is required for anyone aged 18–69 fishing in NSW tidal (saltwater) or inland waters. The fee is the same for residents and non-residents. Licence-free fishing in some community fishing areas. Bag and size limits apply to all species in all Australian waters. The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park (QLD) and other marine parks have additional zoning restrictions. Fishing in no-take zones carries heavy penalties. Check the relevant state fisheries authority before fishing, as regulations change seasonally.
laws.penalty: Fishing without required licence: fine $200–$2,200 depending on state; fishing in prohibited zones: fine up to $100,000 in marine parks
exceptions: Children under a threshold age (varies by state — typically under 18 exempt)
Indigenous Australians exercising traditional fishing rights
Fishing in designated community fishing areas

quiz.q: Does fishing in Victoria cost more for interstate visitors than for local residents?
options: No — same fee applies to all
Interstate visitors do not need any licence
Only freshwater fishing requires a licence
quiz.explanation: In Victoria, interstate visitors pay no more than residents for recreational fishing licences. Australian states don't impose 'non-resident' surcharges.

laws.title: Game Hunting Licence & Hunter Education Requirement
laws.subtitle: Hunter education course required before first game licence is issued
laws.fullDescription: NSW does not use a US-style draw tag system. Hunters must obtain a Game Hunting Licence (GHL) — a general licence covering deer, pigs, foxes, rabbits, and hares on approved land. No annual "tag quota" draw applies. Hunter education (a one-day NSW Hunter Education course) is required before a first GHL is issued. Unlike US systems with annual 'draw' tags and quotas for specific animals, Australian game licensing is generally open to anyone who completes the required education and pays the licence fee. Deer populations are managed through season dates and bag limits rather than tag draws. Landowner permission is always required for hunting on private land.
laws.penalty: Hunting without GHL: fine up to $22,000; GHL without hunter education: application refused
exceptions: Landowners/managers hunting on their own land may have modified requirements
Professional pest controllers operate under different licensing

quiz.q: In Australian states, how is hunting of deer typically regulated?
options: A 'draw' tag system like in the US — limited tags issued by lottery
Open season with a game licence — no annual draw
No licence required — deer are pests
Tag system with fees based on trophy size
quiz.explanation: Australian states do not use US-style annual draw tags. Hunters obtain a general game licence, complete hunter education, and hunt during declared open seasons subject to bag limits. Landowner permission is always required.

laws.title: Waterfowl & Duck Hunting — Seasonal Rules
laws.subtitle: Victoria: Open season (annual dates set by Game Management Authority)
laws.fullDescription: Victoria is one of only three states (with SA and TAS) where recreational duck hunting is permitted. The annual season opens on the first Saturday in April. Bag limits and species permitted are declared annually by the Game Management Authority based on population surveys. A game licence and duck stamp are required. Australia is a signatory to the JAMBA and CAMBA migratory bird agreements with Japan, China, and South Korea, protecting certain migratory species year-round. All native birds are protected under national and state legislation — only specifically declared game species may be hunted during open seasons.
laws.penalty: Killing native waterfowl without a licence: fine up to $22,000 + possible imprisonment
exceptions: Traditional hunting by Indigenous Australians for cultural purposes with authority
Licensed pest control of introduced species (not native waterfowl)

quiz.q: Is recreational duck hunting permitted in Victoria?
options: Yes — but only for residents, not visitors
quiz.explanation: In Victoria: Open season (annual dates set by Game Management Authority). Duck hunting is only permitted in Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania, and (by permit) the NT. It is prohibited in NSW, QLD, WA, and the ACT.

laws.title: Feeding & Baiting Wildlife — Prohibited in Protected Areas
laws.subtitle: Feeding native wildlife in parks is banned; alters behaviour and spreads disease
laws.fullDescription: Feeding wildlife in NSW national parks and reserves is prohibited and can be fined. Feeding alters animal behaviour, causes dependency, spreads disease, and can lead to aggressive behaviour. Specific bans apply at popular tourist sites. Baiting (poisoning) feral animals requires a permit. Common problems caused by tourist feeding include: kangaroos and wallabies becoming aggressive and dependent on handouts; possums developing diabetes from unsuitable food; introduced bird species outcompeting natives when baited. Wildlife carers with authorisation may feed injured animals. Domestic pet food, bread, and processed foods are particularly harmful to native wildlife.
laws.penalty: Feeding wildlife in a national park: on-the-spot fine $300 (penalty notice); prosecuted offence: up to $3,300
exceptions: Licensed wildlife carers treating injured animals
Scientific research with appropriate permits
Farmers using approved baiting methods for pest control (separate permit required)

quiz.q: Why is feeding native wildlife in Australian national parks prohibited?
options: It is not prohibited — feeding is encouraged for tourism
It causes dependency, disease spread, and behavioural problems
It is only prohibited for certain species
quiz.explanation: Feeding native wildlife in protected areas causes serious harm: animals become dependent on human food (often nutritionally wrong), lose fear of humans, spread disease, and may become aggressive. Fines apply in all states.

laws.title: Open Alcohol Container in a Vehicle — Prohibited
laws.subtitle: All occupants prohibited from having an open/unsealed alcohol container in the passenger area
laws.fullDescription: It is an offence in NSW for any person in a motor vehicle to consume liquor or to have an open, unsealed container of liquor accessible in the passenger area. Sealed, unopen alcohol may be transported. A person in a stationary vehicle parked in a public place is also captured. This applies to both moving and stationary vehicles parked in a public place. Sealed, factory-sealed bottles or cans may be transported in the passenger area. In practice, alcohol being consumed or a recently opened container are the main targets. In some states, the rule applies even if the vehicle is parked and the engine is off.
laws.penalty: $1,100 fine (first offence); $2,200 (subsequent)
exceptions: Sealed (factory-sealed) alcohol containers
Limousines and party buses with appropriate licences in some jurisdictions
Alcohol carried in the boot (trunk) of the vehicle

quiz.q: Is it legal to have an open bottle of alcohol in the passenger area of a car in Australia?
options: Yes — if the driver is not drinking
No — open containers are prohibited for all occupants
Yes — if the vehicle is stationary
Only beer is prohibited; wine is permitted
quiz.explanation: Open alcohol containers are prohibited in the passenger area of vehicles across Australia. This applies to all occupants, not just the driver. Sealed factory bottles are permitted.

laws.title: Public Intoxication & Disorderly Conduct
laws.subtitle: Being drunk in public may lead to detention; disorderly behaviour is a criminal offence
laws.fullDescription: Under the Law Enforcement (Powers and Responsibilities) Act 2002, police may detain a person who is intoxicated and unable to care for themselves or behaving in a disorderly manner. They can be placed in a "sobering-up" facility (or taken home) for up to 6 hours. It is an offence to be drunk and disorderly in a public place. Australia's approach has moved away from criminalising intoxication per se toward a harm-reduction model in most states — the focus is on protecting the intoxicated person and the public, rather than automatic prosecution for being drunk. Disorderly conduct, however, remains a criminal offence across all states.
laws.penalty: $220 fine for offensive conduct while intoxicated; up to $1,100 for disorderly behaviour
exceptions: Persons on private property
Medical conditions mimicking intoxication (diabetic episodes, neurological events)

quiz.q: In most Australian states, what happens if a person is found to be heavily intoxicated in a public place but not causing a disturbance?
options: They are automatically charged with a criminal offence
They may be detained for safety and taken to a sobering-up facility or home
They receive an automatic fine with no other action
Nothing — public intoxication alone is not addressed by law
quiz.explanation: Most Australian states take a harm-reduction approach. A very intoxicated person may be detained for their own safety and taken to a sobering shelter or home, rather than automatically charged. Disorderly behaviour associated with intoxication is still a criminal matter.

laws.title: Cannabis — Possession, Purchase & Cross-Border Transport
laws.subtitle: Cannabis illegal; criminal offence
laws.fullDescription: Cannabis is illegal to possess, use, or supply in Victoria. The Drug Dependence Act and Drugs, Poisons and Controlled Substances Act apply. First-time possession of small amounts may attract a caution. ACT's legal personal-use cannabis scheme does not extend to VIC — transporting cannabis from ACT to VIC is illegal under both state and federal law.
laws.penalty: Possession: expiation/fine or up to 2 years imprisonment (varies by state and amount); Supply: up to 15–25 years; Cross-border trafficking: Federal Criminal Code penalties (up to life for commercial quantities)
exceptions: Medical cannabis with valid prescription from a TGA-authorised prescriber
ACT: personal use and home cultivation for adults 18+ (but sale remains illegal and federal land excluded)
SA: cannabis expiation notice scheme for ≤100g personal possession

quiz.q: If a person legally possesses cannabis in the ACT and drives to NSW with it, what applies?
options: NSW law applies — it is illegal
ACT law still applies since they legally obtained it
Federal law applies — it is illegal regardless
It depends on how much they are carrying
quiz.explanation: Transporting cannabis across state/territory borders is a federal offence under the Criminal Code Act 1995, regardless of the laws of the originating or destination jurisdiction. Federal penalties apply.

laws.title: Smoking in Public Places & Outdoor Areas
laws.subtitle: Smoke-free laws cover enclosed venues, outdoor dining, playgrounds & more
laws.fullDescription: The Tobacco Act 1987 prohibits smoking in enclosed public places and workplaces. Outdoor dining areas are smoke-free. Additional restrictions: within 10m of children's playgrounds, at skate parks and outdoor pools, and in bus shelters. Health promotion zones around hospitals prohibit smoking on approach. E-cigarettes (vaping) are now also regulated — in most Australian states, vaping in smoke-free areas is subject to the same rules as smoking following 2023 federal reforms that banned the importation of non-prescription vapes. Prescription nicotine vapes must be obtained from a pharmacy.
laws.penalty: Smoking in prohibited area: $200–$500 individual fine; failure to comply with directions: additional penalties; businesses: $1,100–$5,000 for non-compliance
exceptions: Private homes and private outdoor spaces
Designated smoking areas where provided (reducing)
Fully enclosed private vehicles without passengers under 18 (most states)

quiz.q: From 2023, how has Australia regulated e-cigarettes (vaping)?
options: Banned for import except via prescription; pharmacy dispensed only
Only banned in enclosed public places
quiz.explanation: From 2024, Australia banned the importation of recreational vapes. Non-prescription nicotine vapes must be obtained via a pharmacy with a valid prescription. Vaping is also prohibited in smoke-free areas in most Australian states.

laws.title: Jaywalking & Pedestrian Signal Rules
laws.subtitle: Crossing within 20m of a pedestrian crossing or traffic lights is an offence
laws.fullDescription: Pedestrians must cross at traffic lights where available. In NSW, a pedestrian commits an offence by crossing a road within 20 metres of a pedestrian crossing or traffic lights (other than at the crossing). The "red man / green man" signals must be obeyed. Crossing against a red pedestrian signal is an offence. These rules have historically been inconsistently enforced in Australia, though enforcement campaigns periodically target CBD areas. The underlying justification is preventing pedestrian-vehicle conflicts near intersections where drivers expect pedestrians to use marked crossings. Unmarked road crossings away from controlled intersections are generally legal if done safely.
laws.penalty: $77 fine for crossing other than at a designated crossing when one is nearby; $77 for crossing against pedestrian signal
exceptions: Crossing at an unmarked location more than 20m from the nearest pedestrian crossing
Crossing at a pedestrian crossing on a green or 'walk' signal
Emergency situations

quiz.q: Under Australian road rules, within what distance of a pedestrian crossing must you use the crossing (not jaywalk)?
quiz.explanation: Australian road rules require pedestrians to use a nearby pedestrian crossing if one exists within 20 metres. Crossing the road within 20m of a crossing (other than at the crossing itself) is an offence — commonly called 'jaywalking'.

laws.title: U-Turns & Left-Turn Lane Restrictions
laws.subtitle: U-turns banned at traffic lights (unless signed); left-turn lanes must turn left
laws.fullDescription: U-turns are permitted in NSW unless: a "No U-Turn" sign is displayed, at an intersection controlled by traffic lights (unless a "U-Turn Permitted" sign is shown), across double centre lines, or where the turn cannot be completed safely. Left-turn only lanes ("Left Lane Must Turn Left") must be obeyed; vehicles in that lane must turn left and cannot proceed straight. 'Left lane must turn left' signs are common at busy intersections in CBD areas. Drivers who wish to proceed straight ahead must select a lane marked for straight travel before the intersection — lane changes at or past the intersection trigger a fine.
laws.penalty: Illegal U-turn: $349 fine + 3 demerit points
exceptions: Authorised emergency vehicles
U-turns at intersections with a 'U-Turn Permitted' sign
U-turns on private property

quiz.q: In Australia, may a driver perform a U-turn at traffic lights?
options: Yes — only if a 'U-Turn Permitted' sign is displayed
No — never permitted at traffic lights
Yes — if no vehicles are coming
quiz.explanation: In Australia, U-turns at traffic lights are NOT permitted unless a 'U-Turn Permitted' sign is displayed. Performing an illegal U-turn attracts a fine and demerit points.

laws.title: Speed Limits — Urban 50 km/h, Rural 100 km/h, Freeway 110 km/h
laws.subtitle: Australia uses kilometres per hour; enforcement by fixed, mobile, and average-speed cameras
laws.fullDescription: Default urban speed limit is 50 km/h (40 km/h in high pedestrian activity areas). Rural roads 100 km/h. Freeways/motorways 100–110 km/h. Average speed cameras are extensively used. Speed cameras are not required to be signed in VIC (unlike some states). Australian speed limits are posted in km/h (kilometres per hour) — an important note for visitors from countries using mph. Speed cameras operate without warning signs in most Australian states (unlike some US states that require warning signs). Tolerance thresholds are very low — even 3–4 km/h over the limit may trigger a penalty.
laws.penalty: Exceeding limit by 1–14 km/h: $123 + 1 demerit point; 15–29: $303 + 3 points; 30–44: $696 + 4 points; 45+: $3,218 + 6 points + court appearance
exceptions: Emergency vehicles responding to incidents (with lights and sirens)
Funeral processions in some circumstances
Vehicles legally moving at the speed of traffic (practical defence, not a legal excuse)

quiz.q: What is the default urban speed limit in Victoria?
quiz.explanation: The default urban speed limit across Australia is 50 km/h (with local roads sometimes 40 km/h). In Victoria, freeways/motorways are 110 km/h. Australia uses km/h — not mph.

laws.title: Snow Chains & Alpine Driving Requirements
laws.subtitle: Victoria: When declared by authorities in alpine snow conditions
laws.fullDescription: In alpine areas (Falls Creek, Mt Hotham, Mt Buller, Mt Baw Baw), chain controls are declared by VicRoads/VicEmergency. Carrying chains is strongly advised; mandatory when chain control signs are displayed. "Fit or turn back" is enforced at entry points. When chain controls are in force, 'Fit or turn back' signs are enforced by police and road workers. Chains must be fitted to the drive wheels. All-wheel-drive vehicles are not exempt from chain controls unless specifically signed. It is recommended to practice fitting chains before entering alpine areas.
laws.penalty: Failing to fit chains when required by a chain control notice: $387 fine; vehicle may be turned back
exceptions: Vehicles with approved all-season or winter tyres where specifically exempted by signage
4WD vehicles exempt only where signs specifically indicate this
Emergency vehicles

quiz.q: Are 4WD vehicles automatically exempt from snow chain requirements in Australian alpine areas?
options: No — 4WD vehicles must also fit chains unless signs specifically exempt them
Only AWD vehicles are exempt, not 4WD
Yes — if they have all-terrain tyres
quiz.explanation: 4WD vehicles are NOT automatically exempt from chain controls in Australian alpine areas. Exemptions only apply where signage specifically states this. 'Fit or turn back' means exactly that — regardless of vehicle type.

laws.title: Parking — Meters, Permits, Clearways & Towing
laws.subtitle: Parking enforced by councils and police; clearway violations can result in immediate towing
laws.fullDescription: Parking regulations in NSW combine state road rules with local council parking enforcement. Metered parking, permit zones, clearways, and loading zones are enforced by council rangers and NSW Police. Towing is authorised for vehicles blocking clearways, hydrants, disability spaces, or no-stopping zones. Impound fees apply. Clearways are marked on major arterials and activate during peak hours — vehicles parked in clearways during active hours are subject to immediate towing. Disability parking spaces require a valid Disability Parking Permit (DPP) displayed. The DPP is transferable across Australian states.
laws.penalty: Common parking fines: $263 (clearway); $561 (disability space without permit); $165 (expired meter in CBD); tow and impound: $200+ retrieval fee
exceptions: Disability Parking Permit holders in designated disability spaces
Emergency vehicles and police
Loading zones during permitted hours for commercial deliveries

quiz.q: Is a Disability Parking Permit (DPP) issued in one Australian state valid in other states?
options: No — each state has its own permits
Yes — DPPs are recognised across all Australian states and territories
Yes — but only for 24 hours in another state
quiz.explanation: Disability Parking Permits are recognised across all Australian states and territories. A DPP issued in Victoria, for example, is valid when parking in NSW, QLD, WA, etc.

laws.title: Drone Use — CASA Regulations Apply Nationwide
laws.subtitle: 5.5 km exclusion zones around controlled airports; max 120m AGL for recreational drones
laws.fullDescription: CASA (Civil Aviation Safety Authority) regulations apply uniformly across all Australian states. Recreational drones under 250g: minimal restrictions but must not fly over people. Drones 250g–25kg: cannot fly above 120m AGL, within 5.5 km of a controlled airport, over crowds, in restricted airspace, or at night without CASA approval. Commercial drone operators require a remote pilot licence (RePL) and operating certificate (ReOC). The OpenSky app shows restricted areas. State governments cannot override CASA federal regulations, so drone rules are identical across all Australian states and territories. The CASA DroneRules app and OpenSky map are free tools showing exclusion zones. Drone registration is required for drones over 250g used for commercial purposes. Recreational drones over 250g must follow sub-2kg rules.
laws.penalty: Operating without required approval: up to $13,750 (individual); $68,750 (corporation)
exceptions: Drones under 250g (follow basic safety rules only)
CASA-licensed operators with appropriate approvals
Authorised research with CASA permission
Emergency services drones
laws.sourceLabel: CASA (Civil Aviation Safety Authority) — applies nationwide

quiz.q: Who regulates drone use in Australia, and do these rules differ between states?
options: Each state has its own drone laws
CASA regulates drones federally — rules are the same in all states
The Australian Federal Police regulate drones
Council by-laws govern all drone use
quiz.explanation: CASA (Civil Aviation Safety Authority) regulates all drone operations in Australia under federal law. The rules are the same across all states and territories — state governments cannot apply separate drone regulations.

laws.title: Residential Noise Ordinance — Quiet Hours
laws.subtitle: Excessive noise prohibited, especially Unreasonable noise: any time; standard complaint guideline 10pm–7am
laws.fullDescription: Environment Protection Act 2017. Unreasonable noise from domestic premises is prohibited at any time. Council and EPA enforcement. Construction: 7am–6pm Mon–Fri, 7am–3pm Sat, prohibited Sundays/public holidays. Penalties increase with repeat complaints. Loud music, power tools, and barking dogs are common complaint sources. Council rangers respond to noise complaints; EPA handles industrial or persistent cases.
laws.penalty: First complaint: warning or $200–$500 penalty notice; repeat offences: up to $2,000–$5,000 (residential); construction outside approved hours: up to $5,000 per day
exceptions: Emergency works (burst pipe, fire)
Licensed events with approved noise management plans
Emergency services

quiz.q: What hours are generally considered 'quiet hours' for residential noise in Victoria?
options: Noise can be made any time
quiz.explanation: Quiet hours in Victoria are approximately Unreasonable noise: any time; standard complaint guideline 10pm–7am. Outside these hours, noise must still not be 'unreasonable' — council officers have discretion to issue fines at any time for genuinely disruptive noise.

laws.title: Rental Bond — Maximum Amount & Lodgement Rules
laws.subtitle: Max: 1 month rent; lodged with Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA)
laws.fullDescription: In Victoria, landlords may require a rental bond (security deposit) of up to 1 month rent. The bond must be lodged with Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) — landlords cannot hold bond money themselves. At lease end, the bond is returned within 14 days if no claim, or disputed through the tenancy authority. Bond claims must be documented and justified.
laws.penalty: Landlord retains bond without authority: fine up to $2,200–$5,000; failure to lodge bond promptly: fine up to $1,100
exceptions: Landlords may make claims for unpaid rent, cleaning, damage beyond fair wear and tear
Tenants may dispute bond claims through the state tenancy authority

quiz.q: Where must a landlord in Victoria lodge a tenant's rental bond?
options: In a trust account at their bank
With the tenant in a joint account
Bonds can be held informally by agreement
quiz.explanation: In Victoria, rental bonds must be lodged with Residential Tenancies Bond Authority (RTBA) — not kept by the landlord. This protects tenants and ensures impartial dispute resolution at end of tenancy.

laws.title: Short-Term Rental (STR) — Licensing & Restrictions
laws.subtitle: Victoria: No state-wide night cap on STR. Councils may impose local restrictions via plann
laws.fullDescription: No state-wide night cap on STR. Councils may impose local restrictions via planning schemes. No mandatory state STR register. Platforms such as Airbnb, Stayz, and Vrbo must comply with state and local rules. Neighbours can complain about STR nuisance; bodies corporate (strata) may pass by-laws restricting or prohibiting STR within their complex. Insurance for STR is important as standard home insurance typically does not cover commercial rental activity.
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed STR where permit required: council fine $500–$5,000; repeated breaches: removal from STR platforms and planning enforcement action
exceptions: Owner-occupied properties renting spare rooms may have reduced obligations in some states
Some regional and rural areas have more permissive STR rules

quiz.q: In Victoria, can a body corporate (strata/apartments) ban short-term rentals in their complex?
options: No — STR is a legal right for all property owners
Yes — bodies corporate may pass by-laws restricting or banning STR
quiz.explanation: Bodies corporate in Australian states may pass by-laws restricting or prohibiting short-term rentals within their complex. This applies regardless of state STR rules — the body corporate by-law is an additional layer of private governance.

laws.title: GST (Goods & Services Tax) — Federal 10% on Most Goods & Services
laws.subtitle: No state sales tax in Australia; GST is federal and uniform at 10%
laws.fullDescription: Australia's Goods and Services Tax (GST) is a federal tax of 10% that applies uniformly across all states and territories. Unlike the US, where states set their own sales tax, all of Victoria (and all Australian states) share the identical 10% GST rate — there is no state-level sales tax on top. GST revenue is distributed to states via the Commonwealth Grants Commission. Key exemptions: fresh unprocessed food, health services, education, and childcare.
laws.penalty: Failure to collect and remit GST when registered: ATO penalties up to 75% of unpaid GST + interest; operating without ABN/GST registration when required: additional penalties
exceptions: Fresh unprocessed food (vegetables, fruit, meat, bread)
Health services (doctors, hospitals, prescription medicines)
Education courses
Childcare services
Exports (zero-rated)

quiz.q: What is the GST (sales tax equivalent) rate in South Australia and all Australian states?
quiz.explanation: Australia's GST is a flat 10% and is set federally — there is no state-level sales tax in any Australian state or territory. This is very different from the US system where states independently set sales tax rates ranging from 0–10%+.

laws.title: Minimum Wage & Overtime — Fair Work Act (Federal)
laws.subtitle: National Minimum Wage $24.10/hr (July 2024); awards may be higher
laws.fullDescription: Australia's National Minimum Wage is set by the Fair Work Commission and applies uniformly across Victoria and all Australian states. From July 2024: $24.10/hour ($915.90/week for full-time). Individual awards and enterprise agreements often set higher rates for specific industries. Penalty rates apply for overtime (typically time-and-a-half after 38 hours/week), weekends, and public holiday work. States cannot set a lower minimum wage than the national rate.
laws.penalty: Underpayment of wages: Fair Work Ombudsman can impose penalties up to $93,900 per contravention (individual); $469,500 (corporation); criminal prosecution for deliberate wage theft in some states
exceptions: Trainee and apprentice rates may be lower under training awards
Some remote/farm workers have different award conditions

quiz.q: Who sets the minimum wage in Australia?
options: The Federal Government / Fair Work Commission
Each industry sets its own minimum
quiz.explanation: Australia's minimum wage is set nationally by the Fair Work Commission — states cannot undercut it. The same minimum wage applies in Sydney, Brisbane, Darwin, and Hobart. Awards (industry standards) often exceed the minimum wage.

laws.title: Workers Compensation — WorkSafe Victoria
laws.subtitle: Mandatory employer insurance for workplace injury; VIC-specific scheme
laws.fullDescription: Victoria's workers compensation scheme is administered by WorkSafe Victoria. All employers must hold a WorkSafe Victoria insurance policy. Covers: weekly compensation (95% of base earnings for 13 weeks, then 80%), medical and like expenses, impairment benefits, and death benefits. Workers who suffer a work-related injury or illness are entitled to: income replacement (if unable to work), medical and rehabilitation costs, and a lump-sum payment for permanent impairment. Workers must notify their employer of the injury as soon as possible and can lodge a claim through their employer.
laws.penalty: Employer operating without required WC insurance: fine $10,000–$55,000 (varies by state); personally liable for all compensation payments if uninsured
exceptions: Self-employed sole traders are generally not required to insure themselves (but may choose to)
Some volunteer and not-for-profit workers have modified coverage

quiz.q: Which body administers workers compensation in Victoria?
quiz.explanation: Workers compensation in Victoria is administered by WorkSafe Victoria. Each Australian state and territory has its own workers compensation scheme — there is no single federal scheme for most workers (federal government employees use Comcare).

laws.title: Non-Compete Clauses — Common Law Restraint of Trade
laws.subtitle: No legislation; courts apply 'reasonableness' test — must be no wider than necessary
laws.fullDescription: In Victoria (and across Australia), non-compete and restraint-of-trade clauses in employment contracts are governed by common law — there is no specific legislation. Courts will enforce a restraint only if it is reasonable in: scope of prohibited activities, geographic area, and duration. Typically, restraints of 3–12 months covering a reasonable area are upheld; broad multi-year or nationwide bans are often struck down. SA courts have historically been stricter. In 2024–25, the Australian Government has been consulting on federal reforms to limit non-compete enforceability.
laws.penalty: Breach of enforceable restraint: injunction (court order to stop); damages for provable losses; costs awarded against the breaching party
exceptions: Senior executives and key personnel have stronger enforceable restraints than general employees
Restraints must be narrowly tailored — courts will not 'blue pencil' an overly broad clause in all states
laws.sourceLabel: Victoria Common Law / Fair Work Act

quiz.q: In Australia, what determines whether a non-compete clause in an employment contract is enforceable?
options: Whether it was signed by the employee
Whether it is 'reasonable' in scope, duration, and geography
The industry in which the employee works
quiz.explanation: Australian courts apply a 'reasonableness' test to non-compete clauses. A restraint that is wider than necessary to protect legitimate business interests will be unenforceable. Courts look at duration, geographic area, and what activities are restricted.

laws.title: Unfair Dismissal & Wrongful Termination — Fair Work Act
laws.subtitle: 21 days to lodge unfair dismissal claim; minimum employment period applies
laws.fullDescription: Under the Fair Work Act 2009, employees in Victoria (covered by the national system) may lodge an unfair dismissal claim with the Fair Work Commission within 21 days of termination if: employed for at least 6 months (12 months for small business employees), and the dismissal was harsh, unjust, or unreasonable. Separate 'general protections' (adverse action) claims protect employees dismissed for exercising workplace rights, taking leave, union membership, or making complaints. Maximum compensation: 26 weeks pay or $89,700 (whichever is lower).
laws.penalty: Successful unfair dismissal claim: reinstatement or compensation up to $89,700 (2024); general protections violations: uncapped compensation + penalties on employer
exceptions: Employees below the minimum employment period (6 months/12 months)
Genuine redundancies with proper process
Serious misconduct — instant dismissal may be justified

quiz.q: How many days does an employee have to lodge an unfair dismissal claim in Australia after being dismissed?
quiz.explanation: Employees must lodge an unfair dismissal application with the Fair Work Commission within 21 days of the dismissal taking effect. This deadline is strict — late lodgement requires exceptional circumstances.

laws.title: Consumer Guarantees — Australian Consumer Law (ACL)
laws.subtitle: Automatic statutory guarantees for goods and services; no need to 'register' warranty
laws.fullDescription: The Australian Consumer Law (ACL), which applies in Victoria and all Australian states, provides automatic consumer guarantees for goods priced under $100,000 (or goods normally purchased for personal, domestic, or household use regardless of price). Guarantees include: acceptable quality, fit for purpose, match description, and spare parts available for reasonable period. These rights cannot be excluded by contract. For a major failure, the consumer can reject the goods and demand a refund. For a minor failure, the supplier can choose to repair, replace, or refund.
laws.penalty: Supplier refusing a valid ACL guarantee claim: state/territory consumer law agency can investigate; penalties up to $1.1 million (corporation) for systemic ACL breaches
exceptions: Second-hand goods sold through private sales (not business)
Goods purchased purely for business/commercial use if >$100,000
Goods damaged by misuse by the consumer

quiz.q: Under Australian Consumer Law, what is a consumer entitled to for a 'major failure' in a product?
options: A choice of refund, replacement, or keeping the product and compensation
Whatever the store's return policy says
quiz.explanation: For a 'major failure' — where a product doesn't work as it should and can't be repaired in reasonable time — the consumer can reject the good and choose a refund, replacement, or keep it with compensation for the drop in value. The store's own return policy cannot reduce these legal rights.

laws.title: Data Breach Notification — Notifiable Data Breaches Scheme
laws.subtitle: Federal: organisations must notify OAIC and affected individuals of eligible breaches
laws.fullDescription: The federal Privacy Act 1988 (Notifiable Data Breaches scheme, from 2018) requires Australian entities with annual turnover >$3 million (and some smaller entities in health, finance, etc.) to notify the OAIC (Office of the Australian Information Commissioner) and affected individuals of a data breach involving personal information that is 'likely to result in serious harm'. Victoria government agencies are additionally covered by the state privacy act: VIC Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014. Notification must be made as soon as practicable after becoming aware of the breach.
laws.penalty: Failure to notify a reportable data breach: up to $3.3 million (repeat/serious offence); OAIC can investigate and require remediation
exceptions: Small businesses under $3M turnover (with exceptions)
De-identified data (no personal information involved)
Breaches where harm is not likely to be serious

quiz.q: What is the threshold for mandatory data breach notification under Australia's federal Privacy Act?
options: Breaches where personal data is lost or exposed and likely to cause serious harm
quiz.explanation: Australia's Notifiable Data Breaches scheme requires notification when personal information is involved in a breach AND the breach is 'likely to result in serious harm'. The OAIC and affected individuals must be notified. Small businesses under $3M turnover are generally exempt (with exceptions).

laws.title: Recording Conversations — Consent Rules in Victoria
laws.subtitle: One-party consent — a participant in a conversation may record it.
laws.fullDescription: Under Surveillance Devices Act 1999 (VIC), One-party consent — a participant in a conversation may record it. The federal Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act 1979 also applies to intercepting private communications — this requires all-party consent for true interception. In practice: if you are a participant in a conversation, Victoria law permits recording it. Publishing a recording without consent may constitute a separate privacy offence regardless of how it was recorded.
laws.penalty: Unlawfully recording a private conversation: fine $10,000–$50,000 and/or imprisonment 1–2 years; publishing an unlawful recording: separate offence with similar penalties
exceptions: Recording with consent of all parties (always permitted)
Recording in a public place where there is no reasonable expectation of privacy
Law enforcement with appropriate warrant

quiz.q: Under Victoria law, can you legally record a phone call or conversation you are a participant in, without telling the other party?
options: Yes — Australia allows one-party consent recording nationwide
No — all states require all-party consent
Depends on the state: yes in VIC
Only if the call is for personal use
quiz.explanation: Recording consent laws differ across Australian states. In Victoria: One-party consent — a participant in a conversation may record it. Western Australia and some other states require all-party consent, while NSW, VIC, QLD, ACT, and NT permit participant (one-party) recording.

laws.title: Defamation Law — Uniform Acts & Anti-SLAPP Reforms
laws.subtitle: Serious harm threshold for corporations; updated defences including public interest
laws.fullDescription: Australian defamation law was harmonised in 2005, with major reforms in 2021 applying across Victoria and all states. Key 2021 changes: corporations with more than 10 employees or turnover >$250,000/year can no longer sue for defamation (only natural persons can). A 'serious harm' threshold now applies — trivial defamation claims are filtered out. New defences include 'public interest' (for journalism and matters of genuine public concern) and 'contextual truth'. Anti-SLAPP provisions in some states allow courts to dismiss proceedings that are an abuse of process to silence critics.
laws.penalty: Successful defamation claim: damages (general and aggravated); injunction to remove defamatory material; court costs; maximum damages have been capped in some states
exceptions: Truth (justification) — a complete defence
Honest opinion on a matter of public interest
Qualified privilege (e.g., statements to authorities)
Absolute privilege (parliamentary proceedings, court proceedings)

quiz.q: After Australia's 2021 defamation law reforms, which of the following can no longer sue for defamation?
options: Large corporations with >10 employees or >$250K turnover
quiz.explanation: The 2021 defamation reforms removed the right of large corporations to sue for defamation — only natural persons and very small businesses (≤10 employees, turnover ≤$250K) can bring defamation claims. This prevents large organisations from using defamation to silence critics.

laws.title: Self-Defence & Use of Force — Criminal Law
laws.subtitle: Force must be believed necessary and proportionate; 'castle doctrine' not in Australian law
laws.fullDescription: In Victoria, self-defence is available as a complete defence to criminal charges when: (1) the defendant genuinely believed their conduct was necessary to defend themselves, another person, or their property; and (2) the response was not excessive (proportionate to the threat). Unlike US 'Stand Your Ground' and 'Castle Doctrine' laws, Australian law does not give a blanket right to use lethal force to defend property, and there is a duty to consider retreat if it is safe to do so (in some formulations). Excessive force loses the self-defence protection.
laws.penalty: If self-defence is established: complete acquittal; if excessive force: defence fails but may reduce liability (provocation/reduced intent in some states); using force not justified: assault, manslaughter, or murder charges
exceptions: Defence of third parties — same self-defence principles apply
Defence of property — force must be minimal and proportionate; lethal force generally not justified for property alone
Resisting an unlawful arrest

quiz.q: Does Australian law include a 'Castle Doctrine' giving homeowners the right to use lethal force against home intruders?
options: Yes — all Australian states have a Castle Doctrine
No — Australian self-defence law requires proportionality and does not provide automatic lethal force rights
Only NSW and VIC have a Castle Doctrine
Yes — but only if the intruder is armed
quiz.explanation: Australia does not have a US-style Castle Doctrine. Self-defence requires that the force used be genuinely believed necessary AND proportionate to the threat. Lethal force to protect property alone is not justified. Excessive force loses the self-defence protection.

laws.title: Firearms Licensing & Safe Storage — National Firearms Agreement
laws.subtitle: All firearms require a licence; safe storage mandatory; semi-autos banned for civilians
laws.fullDescription: Following the 1996 Port Arthur massacre, Australia introduced the National Firearms Agreement (NFA). In Victoria, under the Firearms Act 1996 (VIC): all firearms must be registered and the owner must hold a valid firearms licence for the appropriate category. Semi-automatic and pump-action rifles/shotguns are prohibited for civilians. Licensed owners must store firearms in an approved locked safe with ammunition stored separately. A 'genuine reason' (sport/target shooting, hunting, primary production, collectors) must be demonstrated for each category of licence.
laws.penalty: Possession without licence: up to 14 years imprisonment; unlawful storage: fine $5,000–$20,000 + confiscation; trafficking prohibited firearms: up to 25 years
exceptions: Police, military, and authorised security personnel
Licensed dealers (Category H)
Historical/antique firearms with appropriate registration

quiz.q: What major change did Australia make to its firearms laws following the 1996 Port Arthur massacre?
options: It banned all civilian firearm ownership
It introduced a national licensing and registration scheme, banning semi-automatic and pump-action long-arms for civilians
It introduced mandatory firearms training — no other changes
quiz.explanation: The 1996 National Firearms Agreement banned semi-automatic and pump-action long-arms for civilians, required licensing and registration for all firearms, mandated safe storage, and funded a buyback of banned weapons. Australia has had no mass shootings on the same scale since.

laws.title: Domestic Violence Protection Orders — Family Violence Intervention Order (FVIO)
laws.subtitle: Victoria: orders available from police or court; interstate recognition
laws.fullDescription: In Victoria, Family Violence Intervention Order (FVIO)s are available under the Family Violence Protection Act 2008 (VIC) to protect victims of domestic, family, or intimate partner violence. Police may issue an interim order on the spot; courts issue final orders after a hearing. Orders can prohibit the respondent from contacting, approaching, or being near the protected person and their home/workplace. Under the National Domestic Violence Order scheme (2017), orders issued in any Australian state or territory are automatically recognised and enforceable nationwide.
laws.penalty: Breaching a protection order: up to 2 years imprisonment and/or fine up to $22,000 (varies by state); police must arrest for breach if witnessed
exceptions: Emergency orders can be issued by police at scene, active immediately
Orders may also protect children and family members named in the order
Order can include exclusion from the shared home

quiz.q: If a domestic violence protection order is issued in NSW, is it automatically enforceable in Victoria?
options: No — only enforceable in the state that issued it
Yes — under the national recognition scheme, DV orders are enforceable in all Australian states and territories
Only if the parties move there together
quiz.explanation: Since 2017, Australia has a national domestic violence order (DVO) recognition scheme. A DVO made in any state or territory is automatically recognised and enforceable in all others — the victim does not need to apply in each new state.

laws.title: Child Abuse Mandatory Reporting — Professionals Must Report
laws.subtitle: Victoria: Mandatory reporters: registered medical practitioners, midwives, regis
laws.fullDescription: Under the Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 (VIC) — replaced by Child Wellbeing and Safety Act 2005, certain professionals (and in the NT, ALL adults) are mandatory reporters of suspected child abuse and neglect. Mandatory reporters must notify the relevant child protection authority if they believe on reasonable grounds that a child has been, or is at risk of being, abused. Reports are made to Child Protection VIC. Mandatory reporters who fail to report face criminal penalties.
laws.penalty: Failure to report by a mandatory reporter: fine up to $5,500 (NSW) or up to 3 years imprisonment (NT); good-faith reports are protected from civil liability
exceptions: Reporters acting in good faith are protected — even if the abuse is not confirmed
Reports can be made anonymously in some cases
Historical abuse (adult reporting abuse they experienced as a child) — encouraged but not mandatory in most states
laws.sourceLabel: Children, Youth and Families Act 2005 (VIC) — replaced by Child Wellbeing and Safety Act 2005

quiz.q: Which Australian territory requires ALL adults (not just professionals) to report suspected child abuse?
quiz.explanation: The Northern Territory is unique in Australia in requiring ALL adults — not just professionals — to report suspected child abuse. This reflects the NT's particular challenges with child welfare in remote communities.

laws.title: Divorce — Federal Law: 12-Month Separation Required
laws.subtitle: Divorce is a federal matter; no residency requirement; 12-month separation is mandatory
laws.fullDescription: Divorce in Victoria (and all of Australia) is governed by the Family Law Act 1975 — a federal law that applies uniformly. The only ground for divorce is the irretrievable breakdown of the marriage, proven by 12 months of separation. No fault needs to be proven. There is no minimum residency requirement in any particular state — just Australian citizen, permanent resident, or domicile. Applications are filed with the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (not a state court). Short marriages (less than 2 years) require attempted counselling.
laws.penalty: Applying for divorce: court filing fee $1,060 (2024); no penalty for the 'applicant' vs 'respondent' distinction; court order made approx. 1 month after filing if uncontested
exceptions: Separation under the same roof may count as the 12 months if circumstances support it
Short marriages (<2 years) must attend counselling first or prove the marriage is irretrievably broken
Divorce is separate from property settlement and parenting orders
laws.sourceLabel: Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (federal)

quiz.q: Which court in Australia handles divorce applications?
options: The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia
Any court with family law jurisdiction
quiz.explanation: Divorce in Australia is handled by the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia — a federal court. State courts (Supreme, District, Magistrates) do not grant divorces. The same court and rules apply whether you live in Darwin or Melbourne.

laws.title: Marital Property Division — 'Just & Equitable' Federal Standard
laws.subtitle: Family Law Act 1975 (federal): contributions + future needs; 50/50 split not guaranteed
laws.fullDescription: Property division on separation in Victoria (and all of Australia) is governed by the Family Law Act 1975. Courts consider: (1) contributions of each party — financial (income, savings) and non-financial (childcare, homemaking); (2) future needs — including age, health, capacity to earn, care of children. There is no automatic 50/50 split — the outcome is whatever is 'just and equitable'. Superannuation (retirement savings) can be split as part of property settlement. Financial agreements (binding financial agreements / prenups) can alter these default rules if properly drafted.
laws.penalty: No penalty for disputing property division — it is a civil process. Legal costs can be high ($10,000–$100,000+) for contested proceedings. Court may order costs against a party who litigates unreasonably.
exceptions: Binding Financial Agreements (pre/post-nuptial) can override default rules if properly signed and witnessed
Short relationships with minimal combined assets may result in close to a 'contributions-based' outcome

quiz.q: Is marital property automatically split 50/50 on divorce in Australia?
options: Yes — Australian law mandates an equal split
No — courts apply a 'just and equitable' test based on contributions and future needs
Yes — unless one party was at fault
No — the higher earner keeps more in all cases
quiz.explanation: There is no automatic 50/50 property split in Australian family law. Courts assess contributions (financial and non-financial) and future needs to reach a 'just and equitable' result. This means outcomes vary significantly based on circumstances.

laws.title: Abortion & Reproductive Health Access — 24 weeks Threshold in Victoria
laws.subtitle: Victoria: Abortion Law Reform Act 2008 (VIC)
laws.fullDescription: Abortion has been decriminalised across all Australian states and territories. In Victoria, under the Abortion Law Reform Act 2008 (VIC), abortion is available on request up to 24 weeks. 24+ weeks: two registered medical practitioners must agree the abortion is appropriate in all circumstances. Conscientious objection by medical practitioners is permitted in most states, but they must refer the patient to a non-objecting practitioner. Medicare covers abortion under the MBS (Medicare Benefits Schedule) at GP and specialist clinics.
laws.penalty: Performing an abortion outside legal parameters: criminal liability for the practitioner (varies by state); access to abortion services is protected from interference — 'safe access zones' of 150m around clinics prohibit protests
exceptions: Up to 24 weeks: accessible on request at registered providers
Safe access zones (150m buffer) protect clinics from harassment in all Australian states
Medicare covers many abortion services

quiz.q: What is the gestational limit for an abortion on request (without additional approvals) in Victoria?
options: No limit — available on request at any stage
quiz.explanation: In Victoria, abortion is legally available on request up to 24 weeks under the Abortion Law Reform Act 2008 (VIC). After this limit, additional medical approvals are required. All Australian states have now decriminalised abortion.

laws.title: Medicare — Public Health Insurance Eligibility
laws.subtitle: Federal scheme: all Australian citizens, permanent residents, and some visa holders
laws.fullDescription: Medicare is Australia's universal public health insurance scheme — it applies identically in Victoria and across all Australian states. Eligibility: Australian citizens, permanent residents, and citizens of countries with reciprocal healthcare agreements (UK, New Zealand, Italy, Belgium, Finland, Ireland, Malta, the Netherlands, Norway, Slovenia, Sweden). Medicare covers: 100% of GP 'bulk-billed' services, 75–85% of out-of-hospital specialist fees, and 100% of public hospital treatment as a public patient. The Medicare Levy (2% of taxable income) funds part of the scheme.
laws.penalty: No penalty for individuals regarding Medicare eligibility — it is an entitlement. Fraudulent Medicare claims: up to $7,500 fine + imprisonment under Criminal Code; doctors face professional deregistration
exceptions: Overseas visitors without a reciprocal agreement must have travel insurance
International students may access Medicare depending on their visa subclass
Private health insurance reduces out-of-pocket costs for extras (dental, optical, physio)

quiz.q: What percentage of a specialist consultation fee does Medicare cover in Australia?
quiz.explanation: Medicare covers 75–85% of the Schedule fee for out-of-hospital specialist consultations. The gap between the Schedule fee and the specialist's actual charge is the patient's out-of-pocket expense. For public hospital treatment as a public patient, Medicare covers 100%.

laws.title: Raw Milk — Illegal for Human Consumption in All Australian States
laws.subtitle: Raw drinking milk banned; VIC 'bath milk' workaround; street food needs council permit
laws.fullDescription: In Victoria and all Australian states, raw (unpasteurised) milk intended for human consumption is illegal to sell under food safety legislation. Victoria technically allows the sale of 'bath milk' (cosmetic product) with a mandatory bittering agent added — a well-known workaround that is found in VIC health food stores. Street food vendors in Victoria must comply with the Food Act and register with their local council. A Food Safety Supervisor certificate is required for most commercial food operations. Home food businesses also require council registration.
laws.penalty: Selling raw milk for human consumption: fine $10,000–$100,000; illness caused: additional charges; operating unlicensed food premises: fine $2,000–$5,000
exceptions: Private consumption of raw milk from your own dairy animals (personal use only)
Cheese and other dairy products made from raw milk for personal consumption
Raw milk in certified aged cheeses (process kills pathogens over time — some exemptions)

quiz.q: Is it legal to sell raw (unpasteurised) milk for human consumption in any Australian state?
options: Yes — it is legal in Victoria and other states
No — raw milk for human consumption is banned across all Australian states
quiz.explanation: Raw milk for human consumption is banned across all Australian states under food safety law. Victoria's 'bath milk' (with bittering agent) is the only partial exception — technically sold as a cosmetic product. Three children became seriously ill from raw milk products in 2014, reinforcing the ban.

laws.title: Home-Based Food Business & Cottage Food Licensing
laws.subtitle: Council registration required; Food Safety Supervisor certificate needed
laws.fullDescription: In Victoria, anyone selling homemade food commercially must register their premises with their local council under the Food Act. This includes: home bakers, jam makers, caterers operating from home, and meal-kit preparers. A Food Safety Supervisor (FSS) certificate is required for the responsible person (a 1–2 day course through a registered training organisation). Home kitchens must meet basic hygiene standards. Some low-risk foods (e.g., shelf-stable baked goods, jams) may have a simplified registration pathway. Home businesses with customers visiting or signage may also need a council planning permit.
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed home food business: council fine $1,000–$5,000; food safety incidents: additional prosecution; insurance: public liability insurance strongly recommended (not legally mandatory in most cases)
exceptions: Very small-scale not-for-profit community food sharing (varies by council)
Cooking classes where no food is sold (no licence needed in most cases)
Church/school fetes may have temporary event food permits

quiz.q: What certification is typically required for someone running a home-based food business in Australia?
options: No qualification required if cooking at home
quiz.explanation: A Food Safety Supervisor (FSS) certificate — a 1–2 day course through a registered training organisation — is required for home food businesses in most Australian states. The business premises (home kitchen) must also be registered with the local council.

laws.title: Professional Licensing — Trades, Construction & Beauty
laws.subtitle: Electricians, plumbers, builders need state licences; beauty services vary
laws.fullDescription: Victoria requires: registered electrician (Energy Safe Victoria), licensed plumber (VBA), registered builder (VBA), real estate agents (Consumer Affairs VIC). Beauty: no specific state licence, but councils may require health premises registration for tattooing and skin penetration. It is illegal for unlicensed persons to carry out licensed trade work in Victoria — this includes simple household electrical work (changing power points, installing light fittings) and plumbing. Owner-builders may be permitted to do certain work on their own property subject to limits and insurance. All licensed tradespeople must carry their licence and show it on request.
laws.penalty: Carrying out unlicensed trade work: fine $5,000–$50,000 (electrical: most serious — electrocution risk); plumbing: $2,000–$20,000; unlicensed building work: owners may be unable to sell or insure property
exceptions: Owner-builders with appropriate owner-builder permits (limited scope)
Students under direct supervision of a licensed tradesperson
Emergency repairs by homeowners (e.g., turning off water at mains)

quiz.q: In Victoria, can a homeowner legally install a new power point or rewire a light switch themselves?
options: Yes — if it's in their own home
No — all electrical work must be done by a licensed electrician
Only for work in rooms they personally own
quiz.explanation: In all Australian states, electrical work must be carried out by a licensed electrician — homeowners cannot legally do their own electrical work (other than changing a light bulb or plug-in appliances). This applies even for simple tasks like adding a power point.

laws.title: Liquor Licence for Restaurants — Victorian Commission for Gambling and Liquor Regulation (VCGLR)
laws.subtitle: On-premises liquor licence required to sell alcohol with meals; separate from food business licence
laws.fullDescription: Restaurants, cafes, and bars in Victoria must hold a separate liquor licence to sell alcohol. The licence is issued by Victorian Commission for Gambling and Liquor Regulation (VCGLR) and specifies: trading hours, patron limits, conditions (e.g., meals must accompany alcohol for some licences), and responsible service of alcohol (RSA) requirements. All staff serving alcohol must hold an RSA certificate. Licence fees and processing times vary. Some councils also impose local conditions. Small bars, clubs, and hotels have different licence categories.
laws.penalty: Serving alcohol without a licence: fine up to $13,000+ and possible criminal charges; RSA breach: licence suspension or cancellation; serving minors: fine $11,000–$33,000 per offence
exceptions: Exempt events (small private functions in private homes)
BYOB restaurants (diners bring their own — different rules apply)
Some religious ceremonies
laws.sourceLabel: Victorian Commission for Gambling and Liquor Regulation (VCGLR) — Victoria

quiz.q: Which body issues liquor licences to restaurants in Victoria?
options: Victorian Commission for Gambling and Liquor Regulation (VCGLR)
quiz.explanation: Liquor licences in Victoria are issued by Victorian Commission for Gambling and Liquor Regulation (VCGLR). This is a state-based process — each state has its own licensing authority. A separate liquor licence is required in addition to a food business registration to legally sell alcohol in a restaurant or café.

laws.title: Sunday & Public Holiday Alcohol Sales — No General Ban in Australia
laws.subtitle: Australia permits 7-day alcohol trading under licence conditions; hours set per licence
laws.fullDescription: Unlike some US and Canadian jurisdictions, Victoria has no general prohibition on Sunday alcohol sales. Licensed premises in Victoria trade during hours specified by their individual licence, 7 days a week. No general Sunday ban. Licensed premises trade during their licensed hours, 7 days a week. Public holiday restrictions are minimal in VIC. Public holiday trading: licensed premises may trade during their standard licensed hours on most public holidays; some states require separate approval for extended trading on Christmas Day or Good Friday. Responsible Service of Alcohol (RSA) applies at all times, including Sundays and public holidays.
laws.penalty: Serving alcohol outside licensed hours: fine $5,000–$20,000 + licence suspension; Good Friday: some states completely prohibit alcohol sales — check local rules
exceptions: Good Friday and Christmas Day restrictions: vary by state — check specific licence conditions
Dry areas and restricted alcohol zones (particularly NT): apply regardless of day
Minors are prohibited from entering licensed premises unsupervised regardless of trading hours
laws.sourceLabel: Victorian Commission for Gambling and Liquor Regulation (VCGLR) — Victoria

quiz.q: Does Australia have a 'Sunday liquor law' preventing alcohol sales on Sundays, like some US states?
options: Yes — all Australian states ban Sunday alcohol sales
Yes — but only in SA and TAS
No — Australian states permit alcohol sales 7 days a week under licence conditions
Yes — but only before midday on Sundays
quiz.explanation: Australia has no general Sunday alcohol sales ban. Licensed premises may sell alcohol 7 days a week during their licensed hours. Some public holidays (particularly Good Friday) have restrictions in some states, but Sunday itself is not restricted across any Australian state.
